strengths: The paper targets a meaningful limitation of reservoir computing: dense recurrent matrices and sequential execution make conventional ESNs poorly suited to modern accelerators. Combining a complex diagonal recurrence, associative scan, and lightweight nonlinear mixing is practically motivated and moderately original in the RC setting.

The empirical study covers memory, synthetic and real-world forecasting, UEA/UCR classification, and sequential/permuted MNIST. ParalESN often substantially improves over shallow ESNs; for example, it reaches 96.2%/96.9% on sMNIST/psMNIST versus 82.5%/78.2% for ESN, while reporting lower runtime and energy.

The diagonal parameterization genuinely reduces reservoir-parameter storage from quadratic to linear in hidden size (apart from input projections), and the measured scaling experiment illustrates a useful practical advantage over the particular dense ESN implementation evaluated.

The manuscript is generally well organized and readable. It documents datasets, hardware, major hyperparameter search ranges, and preprocessing, includes sensitivity analysis, and compares against two other structured reservoir constructions.
No material research-ethics concern is apparent. Measuring energy and emissions is a positive addition, although the interpretation requires qualifications.
weaknesses: Soundness: Proposition 4.2 is false as stated. The proof asserts an exact decomposition W_h=VΛV^{-1} after noting that an arbitrary square matrix is diagonalizable only up to an arbitrarily small perturbation. Defective matrices are not diagonalizable, so the claimed exact, same-dimension equivalence for every linear reservoir and every input does not follow. Approximate diagonalization after perturbation would require an approximation/error and stability argument that is absent. This directly undermines the advertised equivalence to arbitrary linear reservoirs.

Soundness: the universality discussion does not establish the result for the implemented architecture. The theoretical model assumes an unrestricted nonlinear MLP readout, whereas the practical model generally uses a randomly fixed, local convolutional tanh mixer followed by a trained linear ridge readout; for MNIST, only the later two-layer MLP readout is trained. No argument shows that this restricted fixed mixer realizes the MLP required by the cited universality result. Thus the broad claim that the proposed practical ParalESN preserves traditional ESN universality is unsupported.

Soundness/presentation: Theorem 4.1 states necessity of |λ_i|<1, but its necessity proof treats only |λ_i|>1 and omits |λ_i|=1. The missing boundary case is easy to repair, but it indicates that the proof does not fully prove the stated theorem.

Complexity claims conflate parallel depth with computational work. Associative scan has O(log T) span only with a number of processors growing with T (the footnote assumes Θ(T/log T) processors), while total work and activation storage remain at least linear in T. Table 5 and repeated prose describe O(log(T)N_hN_in) as whole-sequence 'time complexity' and say the linear dependence on sequence length is removed without clearly fixing the parallel computation model. The abstract/conclusions consequently overstate computational savings.

The efficiency comparison is incomplete and potentially favorable to ParalESN. Dense ESNs are used as the principal baseline even though sparse and structured ESNs are common; SCR and Structured RC receive only a small forecasting accuracy comparison, with no corresponding timing, memory, large-reservoir, or classification results. The out-of-memory result therefore does not establish an advantage over scalable RC implementations generally.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the extensive empirical claims. The manuscript does not state the number of random seeds underlying mean±deviation, identify whether the deviations are standard deviations or errors, report selected hyperparameters/configurations, specify the Bayesian optimization implementation and number of trials, or provide code for ParalESN. A 24-hour search limit alone does not define a reproducible or demonstrably equal search budget.

Reported training time and energy appear to exclude the potentially substantial Bayesian model-selection cost, despite ParalESN having many sensitive reservoir and mixer hyperparameters. Figure 6 itself shows strong sensitivity to spectral radius, phase, leakage, and mixer scale. Consequently, claims of orders-of-magnitude training/energy savings describe fitting a selected configuration rather than the full learning workflow and should be qualified.

The statistical analysis is underspecified. The paper calls Figure 3 a 'critical difference plot computed via a Wilcoxon test' but gives neither the test unit, sample count, significance level, multiple-comparison correction, nor enough per-task ranks to verify its cliques. The statement of a statistically significant advantage is therefore not adequately supported.

Significance is limited by the evaluation regime. Comparisons with fully trained LSTM/Transformer/LRU/Mamba models occur only on sMNIST and psMNIST, relatively old synthetic sequence benchmarks; the real-world forecasting and UEA/UCR experiments compare only RC variants. There is no modern long-sequence benchmark demonstrating that the proposed scan yields useful accuracy/throughput tradeoffs at realistic scale.

Originality is moderate rather than high: diagonal complex linear recurrences and associative scans are inherited directly from LRUs/SSMs, while random reservoirs and fixed nonlinear feature maps are established ideas. Recasting their combination for reservoir computing is useful, but the paper currently overstates the theoretical novelty and guarantees.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant scalability problem in reservoir computing and presents a conceptually simple architecture combining diagonal complex-valued recurrence, associative scans, and lightweight nonlinear mixing.

The empirical study covers memory, synthetic forecasting, real-world forecasting, time-series classification, and sequential MNIST tasks. Tables 1–4 generally show that ParalESN is substantially faster than dense ESNs while remaining competitive in predictive performance.
The comparison reports runtime, energy consumption, and estimated emissions, and Appendix B makes the processor assumption behind the claimed logarithmic parallel depth explicit.
The manuscript is visually polished and mostly easy to follow. The architecture, initialization, datasets, broad hyperparameter search spaces, and computational hardware receive useful descriptions.
The work is a potentially useful reservoir-computing adaptation of ideas from LRUs and structured state-space models, although its methodological originality is modest.
weaknesses: The central exact-expressivity result is unsound. Proposition 4.2 claims equivalence to an arbitrary linear reservoir by diagonalizing its transition matrix, but its proof says that every matrix is diagonalizable only up to an arbitrarily small perturbation and then proceeds as though an exact decomposition W_h=VΛV^{-1} always existed. Defective matrices, including Jordan blocks, are counterexamples. Consequently, the claimed exact equivalence and the universality corollary are not established by the provided argument.

Theorem 4.1 is also incompletely proved: the necessity argument treats only |λ_i|>1 and omits the boundary case |λ_i|=1, despite claiming an if-and-only-if condition. More broadly, the theory studies a ParalESN with an unrestricted MLP readout, whereas the implemented model uses a fixed random convolutional mixer and trains only the final readout. No result shows that this restricted practical architecture inherits the stated universality guarantee.

The complexity presentation conflates parallel depth with total computation. The O(log(T)N_hN_in) result assumes Θ(T/log T) processors, while total work and storage of all states remain linear in T. Calling this the whole-sequence 'time complexity' and repeatedly stating that dependence on sequence length is reduced from linear to logarithmic overstates what is obtained on finite hardware.

The experimental evidence is insufficiently reproducible. The paper provides no code or artifact statement, selected hyperparameter configurations, random seeds, number of repetitions, Bayesian-search implementation or budget in evaluations, or uncertainty definition. Important data-generation details such as numerical solvers and sampling intervals for chaotic systems are absent.

Several task and metric definitions are unclear. The ETT experiments state a 'delay of 192' without clearly specifying input context, forecast horizon, window construction, or the metric reported in Table 2. The regression tables likewise do not clearly label the error metric, making comparison or replication difficult.

Baseline fairness is not convincing. Fully trainable models are compared only on sMNIST/psMNIST, use fixed architecture choices with primarily learning-rate and weight-decay tuning, and are trained for up to 100 epochs, whereas reservoir models receive extensive architecture-specific Bayesian searches lasting up to 24 hours. Search cost is excluded from the reported training-time and energy comparisons. The meaning of the approximately equal parameter counts in Table 4 is also unclear, particularly whether untrained reservoir parameters are counted.

The strongest empirical claims are broader than the results support. On forecasting, ParalESN frequently only matches or underperforms the dense ESN variants; modern trainable forecasting baselines are absent. The normalized aggregate plots use min–max scaling relative to one baseline, while the multiple-comparison correction and construction of the Wilcoxon-based significance cliques are not specified.

There is no dedicated limitations discussion. The paper does not adequately discuss the large O(TN_h) activation memory, dependence on extensive hyperparameter tuning demonstrated in Figure 6, limited task domains, restricted nonlinear mixer, hardware dependence of scan speedups, or uncertainty in CodeCarbon emissions estimates. Ethical risk is otherwise low, and reporting energy use is welcome, but this does not remedy the technical and evidential deficiencies.

strengths: Significance: ParalESN addresses genuine scalability problems in reservoir computing. Its diagonal recurrence reduces parameter storage, and associative scans produce convincing empirical speedups across sequence lengths while retaining competitive predictive performance.

Empirical scope: The evaluation covers memory, synthetic and real-world forecasting, UEA/UCR classification, and sequential/permuted MNIST. ParalESN substantially outperforms conventional ESNs on several classification tasks and approaches trained LSTM, Transformer, LRU, and Mamba models on the MNIST variants at much lower reported training cost.

Originality: Combining an untrained complex diagonal recurrence, LRU-inspired initialization, lightweight random convolutional mixing, and a trained readout is a coherent and useful synthesis. The result is more than a simple sparse ESN, although most individual ingredients are established.

Presentation and ethics: The manuscript is well organized and visually polished, with clear architectural diagrams, readable tables, computational-resource disclosure, and energy/emissions measurements. weaknesses: Soundness: Proposition 4.2 is false as stated. Its proof assumes an exact decomposition Wh=VΛV^{-1} for every square matrix, whereas defective matrices are not diagonalizable, including over the complex field. The observation that such matrices can be arbitrarily perturbed does not establish the claimed exact equality of outputs. An approximation theorem would require explicit error control, stability assumptions, and potentially altered dimensions. Consequently, the stated equivalence to arbitrary linear reservoirs and the derivation of Corollary 4.3 are not currently supported.

The proof of the necessary direction of Theorem 4.1 treats only |λ|>1, omitting the boundary |λ|=1 despite claiming an if-and-only-if result. This boundary is easy to handle, but the written proof is incomplete.

Complexity claims conflate parallel depth with total computation. Associative scan has logarithmic span only with a growing number of processors—the appendix assumes Θ(T/log T) processors—while total work and activation storage remain linear in T. Labeling O(log(T)NhNin) simply as whole-sequence time complexity and stating that the linear dependence on T is removed overstates the result for fixed hardware.

The evidence does not isolate which proposed components cause the accuracy gains. There are no controlled ablations of complex versus real recurrence, eigenvalue initialization, the nonlinear convolutional mixer, row scaling, or depth, nor a direct untrained-LRU/random-feature SSM baseline. ParalESN also receives a substantially richer hyperparameter search space than the ESN baseline, so the source of the reported gains is unclear.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the quantitative claims. The paper gives search ranges and hardware but not the number of runs, random seeds, Bayesian-search trial counts, selected configurations per dataset, reservoir sizes for Table 4, batching and timing protocol, implementation details of the scan, or an artifact for the proposed method. It is also unclear whether hyperparameter-search cost is excluded from the reported training and energy measurements.

The statistical summary needs more care: the number of repetitions underlying each mean and deviation is unspecified, and the critical-difference-style plot is described as using Wilcoxon tests without explaining multiple-comparison correction. Min-max-normalized percentage improvements across heterogeneous metrics can also exaggerate aggregate differences.

Significance is demonstrated mainly against traditional RC, while comparisons to modern trainable sequence models are limited to two MNIST-derived tasks. Broader long-sequence benchmarks and stronger structured/random-feature baselines are needed to establish the claimed pathway into contemporary deep learning.

The manuscript contains no dedicated limitations discussion. Important caveats—finite-processor scan behavior, linear activation memory, hyperparameter sensitivity, reliance on a nonlinear readout for the theory, and the gap between the theoretical MLP-readout model and ridge-readout experiments—should be stated explicitly.
